_note: Curated example projects: small, beginner-friendly gadgets that protect your own home network, accounts and spaces. Shown in the gallery (CLI --gallery, web 'Gallery' tab) and used by the offline mock provider. Same shape as what the LLM returns, plus id + tags (+ optional tutorial link).

projects.title: Pi-hole Ad Blocker
projects.summary: A tiny Raspberry Pi that blocks ads and trackers for every device on your home Wi-Fi (phones, laptops, smart TVs) by acting as your network's DNS server.

steps.title: Flash the SD card
steps.detail: In Raspberry Pi Imager choose Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). In the settings set a hostname (pihole), your Wi-Fi, a username and password, and enable SSH. Write the card.

steps.title: Boot and connect
steps.detail: Put the card in the Pi, power it, wait two minutes, then from your computer run: ssh <username>@pihole.local

steps.title: Give it a fixed address
steps.detail: In your router's admin page, find the Pi in the list of connected devices and add a DHCP reservation, so its IP address never changes.

steps.title: Install Pi-hole
steps.detail: Update first (sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y), then run the official installer: curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | bash. Accept the defaults and note the admin address it shows at the end.

steps.title: Set the admin password
steps.detail: Run sudo pihole setpassword, then open http://pihole.local/admin in a browser and log in to the dashboard.

steps.title: Point your network at it
steps.detail: In the router's DHCP/DNS settings, set the Pi's IP address as the only DNS server. Reconnect your devices to Wi-Fi so they pick up the change.

steps.title: Test and tune
steps.detail: Open a news site: ads should be gone and the dashboard's 'Queries blocked' counter should rise. If a site breaks, find its domain in Query Log and click Allow.

safetyNotes: If the Pi is off, websites stop loading for everyone. Plug it into a reliable socket, or keep a note of how to switch the router's DNS back.
Don't add a public DNS server as a second DNS in the router: devices would use it to go around Pi-hole.

projects.title: Home VPN with WireGuard
projects.summary: Your own VPN server at home: on public Wi-Fi your phone sends everything through an encrypted tunnel to your house, and gets your Pi-hole ad blocking on the go.

parts.name: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W
parts.purpose: VPN server (a Raspberry Pi 4 with Ethernet is faster)

steps.title: Prepare the Pi
steps.detail: Flash Raspberry Pi OS Lite with SSH enabled (as in the Pi-hole build) and give the Pi a DHCP reservation in your router. You can run the VPN on the same Pi as Pi-hole.

steps.title: Install WireGuard
steps.detail: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y wireguard qrencode. Then create keys for the server and your phone: wg genkey | tee server.key | wg pubkey > server.pub (repeat with phone.key / phone.pub).

steps.title: Write the server config
steps.detail: Create /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf with Address = 10.8.0.1/24, ListenPort = 51820, the server private key, and a [Peer] for the phone (its public key, AllowedIPs = 10.8.0.2/32). Add PostUp/PostDown iptables MASQUERADE rules so the phone can reach the internet through the Pi.

steps.title: Turn on forwarding and start
steps.detail: Set net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 in /etc/sysctl.conf (apply with sudo sysctl -p), then sudo systemctl enable --now wg-quick@wg0.

steps.title: Open one port
steps.detail: In the router, forward UDP port 51820 to the Pi's IP. If your home IP changes, set up a free dynamic-DNS name (for example DuckDNS) for it.

steps.title: Connect your phone
steps.detail: Write phone.conf (Address = 10.8.0.2/32, DNS = the Pi's IP, the server's public key, Endpoint = your-home-address:51820, AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0), show it as a QR code with qrencode -t ansiutf8 < phone.conf and scan it in the WireGuard app.

steps.title: Test from outside
steps.detail: Switch the phone to mobile data, turn the tunnel on and open a website. The WireGuard app shows data flowing; sudo wg on the Pi shows the phone's latest handshake.

safetyNotes: Forward only UDP 51820, nothing else, and keep the Pi updated (sudo apt full-upgrade).
Treat phone.conf like a password: delete it from the Pi after scanning, and remove a lost phone's [Peer] block straight away.

projects.title: DIY Security Key
projects.summary: Turn a Raspberry Pi Pico into a FIDO2 USB security key you can use for passkeys and two-factor login, with open-source firmware.

parts.name: USB cable
parts.purpose: connects it to your computer (data cable, not charge-only)

parts.name: Small case or heat-shrink tube
parts.purpose: protects the board on your keyring

steps.title: Download the firmware
steps.detail: From the pico-fido project's Releases page on GitHub, download the .uf2 file built for your board (Raspberry Pi Pico / RP2040).

steps.title: Flash it
steps.detail: Hold the white BOOTSEL button while plugging the Pico in. It appears as a USB drive called RPI-RP2; drag the .uf2 file onto it. The board restarts as a security key.

steps.title: Set a PIN
steps.detail: In Chrome go to Settings → Privacy and security → Security → Manage security keys → Create a PIN (Windows: Settings → Accounts → Sign-in options → Security key).

steps.title: Try it safely
steps.detail: Open webauthn.io, register, then log in. When the browser asks you to touch the key, press the BOOTSEL button, which pico-fido uses as the 'touch' confirmation.

steps.title: Use it on a real account
steps.detail: Add it as an extra security key on an account that supports passkeys or FIDO2 (Google, GitHub, Microsoft). Keep your existing 2FA method as a backup.

steps.title: Make it pocket-proof
steps.detail: Slide the board into a small case or heat-shrink tube and put it on your keyring.

safetyNotes: This is a learning project: the Pico has no secure chip, so someone with the key in hand could read its secrets. Always keep a backup login method.

projects.title: 2FA Code Display
projects.summary: A desk gadget that shows your rotating 6-digit two-factor codes (TOTP, like Google Authenticator) on a small screen, with a countdown bar.

parts.name: ESP32 dev board
parts.purpose: gets the exact time over Wi-Fi and computes the codes

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: OLED: VCC→3V3, GND→GND, SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22. Button between GPIO4 and GND (use INPUT_PULLUP).

steps.title: Get the exact time
steps.detail: Connect to Wi-Fi and call configTime(0, 0, "pool.ntp.org"). TOTP codes only match if the clock is right to within a few seconds.

steps.title: Add a test secret
steps.detail: When a site shows you a 2FA QR code, it also offers the secret as text (Base32). Start with a test account, decode the Base32 secret to bytes and store it in your sketch.

steps.title: Compute the code
steps.detail: Use a TOTP library (for example TOTP-Arduino), or follow RFC 6238 yourself: HMAC-SHA1 of the 30-second time step, dynamic truncation, last 6 digits.

steps.title: Draw the screen
steps.detail: With the Adafruit SSD1306 library: account name on top, the 6-digit code in big digits, and a bar that shrinks over the 30 seconds.

steps.title: Check against your phone
steps.detail: Add the same test secret to your phone's authenticator app. Both should show the same code at the same moment.

safetyNotes: The secret is stored in the ESP32's flash in plain form. Use it for test or low-value accounts, keep the device at home, and keep your phone app as the main 2FA.

projects.title: Hardware Password Generator
projects.summary: Press a button, get a strong random password or passphrase on a small screen, made by the ESP32's hardware random-number generator. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere.

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: OLED on I2C (SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22, VCC→3V3, GND→GND). Buttons from GPIO4 and GPIO5 to GND, INPUT_PULLUP.

steps.title: Use real randomness
steps.detail: Call esp_random() for random numbers. It is a true hardware RNG while Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is on; with radios off, call bootloader_random_enable() first.

steps.title: Pick characters fairly
steps.detail: For each character, draw a random number and reject it if it falls above the largest multiple of your alphabet size (rejection sampling), so no character is more likely than another.

steps.title: Passphrase mode
steps.detail: The second button switches to 5 random words from a word list (for example the EFF short word list stored in flash): easier to type, still strong.

steps.title: Show the strength
steps.detail: Display the length and the entropy in bits (length × log2(alphabet size)). Aim for at least 80 bits.

safetyNotes: Type the password straight into your password manager and press the button again so it disappears from the screen.

projects.title: RFID Access Lock
projects.summary: Tap the right card and a servo opens the latch on your drawer or box; tap the wrong one and it beeps red. After 5 wrong tries it locks out for 30 seconds.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: checks the card and drives the latch

parts.name: RC522 RFID reader + tags
parts.purpose: reads the card or key fob

steps.title: Wire the reader
steps.detail: RC522 runs on 3.3 V: 3.3V→3.3V (not 5V!), GND→GND, RST→D9, SDA(SS)→D10, MOSI→D11, MISO→D12, SCK→D13.

steps.title: Wire latch, LEDs and buzzer
steps.detail: Servo signal→D6, red→5V, brown→GND. Green LED→D7, red LED→D8 through 220 Ω resistors. Buzzer + →D5, − →GND.

steps.title: Read your card IDs
steps.detail: Install the MFRC522 library, upload the sketch and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. Tap each card; it prints its UID.

steps.title: Allow your cards
steps.detail: Copy the UIDs of the cards you want to accept into the ALLOWED list at the top of the sketch and upload again.

steps.title: Build the latch
steps.detail: Glue the servo inside the box lid so its horn swings behind a small block on the box wall. Find the 'open' and 'closed' angles and set them in the sketch.

steps.title: Test the lockout
steps.detail: Tap an unknown card 5 times: the red LED should blink and every card is ignored for 30 seconds.

safetyNotes: A card's UID alone is easy to copy with a cheap cloner, so this is a learning lock for a drawer, not for a door.
Keep a way to open the box without the reader (a hidden screw), in case the battery or code fails.

projects.title: Door Tamper Alarm
projects.summary: A magnetic sensor on your door or drawer: when it's opened while armed, the ESP32 beeps and sends a notification to your phone.

parts.name: ESP32 dev board
parts.purpose: watches the sensor, sends the alert over Wi-Fi

steps.title: Wire the sensor
steps.detail: Reed switch between GPIO27 and GND, with INPUT_PULLUP. Door closed (magnet near) = LOW, door open = HIGH.

steps.title: Wire buzzer, LED and button
steps.detail: Buzzer on GPIO25, LED through 220 Ω on GPIO26, button from GPIO4 to GND (INPUT_PULLUP).

steps.title: Arm and disarm
steps.detail: The button toggles 'armed'. Give yourself 20 seconds to leave after arming, and 15 seconds after the door opens to disarm before the alarm goes off.

steps.title: Phone notifications
steps.detail: Install the free ntfy app and subscribe to a long random topic name. On alarm, the ESP32 sends an HTTP POST to https://ntfy.sh/<your-topic> with the message 'Door opened!'.

steps.title: Mount it
steps.detail: Stick the reed switch on the frame and the magnet on the door, less than 1 cm apart when closed. Test that opening the door triggers it.

safetyNotes: Anyone who knows an ntfy topic name can read it, so use a long random name and don't put personal details in messages.

projects.title: Ad-Blocker Status Light
projects.summary: A small LED bar on your shelf that glows greener the more ads and trackers your Pi-hole is blocking, and turns red if Pi-hole goes offline.

parts.name: ESP32 dev board
parts.purpose: asks Pi-hole for its stats over Wi-Fi

parts.name: WS2812B addressable LED strip (1 m)
parts.purpose: cut a piece with 8 LEDs for the bar

parts.name: Resistor
parts.purpose: 330 Ω on the LED data line

steps.title: You need a Pi-hole
steps.detail: Build the Pi-hole Ad Blocker first. In its web settings, create an app password for the API.

steps.title: Wire the LEDs
steps.detail: LED strip 5V→VIN (USB 5 V), GND→GND, DIN→330 Ω→GPIO13. 8 LEDs at low brightness are fine on USB power.

steps.title: Log in to the API
steps.detail: Pi-hole v6: POST {"password": "<app password>"} to http://pi.hole/api/auth and keep the session ID it returns (see http://pi.hole/api/docs).

steps.title: Read the stats
steps.detail: Every 30 seconds GET http://pi.hole/api/stats/summary with the X-FTL-SID header and read queries.percent_blocked.

steps.title: Show it
steps.detail: With FastLED, light 1 LED per ~5 % blocked, from yellow to green. If the request fails 3 times in a row, blink all LEDs red.

safetyNotes: Keep the app password only on the ESP32 and your home network; don't publish the sketch with it inside.
